name: skia-canvas
baseline: node-canvas (the npm 'canvas' package v3.2.3, which renders with Cairo)
workload: Node.js Canvas 2D API test scripts in the samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks repo (Path2D drawing, Bezier curves, dense line chart, SVG to PNG/SVG/PDF, PDF to PNG, scale/rotate images, get/put ImageData, gradients, text, cold start), each timed over 20-250 iterations with the Cairo-based canvas package as the 1.0x baseline.
claimed_speedup: Relative to canvas (Cairo) = 1.0x, skia-canvas serial / async: Path2D 45 ms vs 133 ms = 3.0x / 20 ms = 6.7x; Bezier curves 9.3x / 39.5x; dense line chart 5.5x / 20.4x; SVG to PNG 4.9x / 12.8x; SVG to PDF 5.6x / 17.0x; scale/rotate images 6.6x / 33.5x; gradients 7.8x / 16.3x; text 1.7x / 5.7x; PDF to PNG 1.7x / 3.0x; get/put ImageData only 1.3x / 1.6x; cold start 7 ms vs 108 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Node 24.6.0; prebuilt npm packages skia-canvas v4.0.0-rc6 and canvas v3.2.3 (also @napi-rs/canvas v1.0.10, canvaskit-wasm v0.42.0); native build flags not stated on the results page; run with `npm install && npm run bench` from the benchmark repo
hardware: MacBook Air 13-inch (M3, 2024, Mac15,12): Apple M3 2.4 GHz 8 cores, 24 GiB RAM, macOS 15.7.5
tradeoffs: Node.js native addon only (also runs in Bun/Deno-style hosts via Node-API); depends on Google Skia built into the addon; adds multi-threaded async rendering, PDF/SVG vector export, and Display P3 colour beyond the browser Canvas API; output PNG sizes differ from node-canvas because it picks adaptive PNG filters.
caveats: Benchmarks were run and published by the skia-canvas author (first-party), with the Cairo-based canvas package as baseline. The 'async' rows start every iteration at once inside Promise.all so they measure multi-threading as well as raster speed, whereas the baseline runs one render at a time; the serial rows are the fairer single-render comparison. The gain mostly reflects Skia versus Cairo rather than a new rasterizer. Image get/put is only 1.3x/1.6x. Tier A is generous: the toolchain is prebuilt npm binaries, so compiler and flags are not stated, but versions, CPU and test code are public. In the SVG to SVG and SVG to PDF tests the canvas and @napi-rs/canvas baselines rasterize the SVG to a bitmap while skia-canvas emits vector output, so those rows are not the same work. The tested skia-canvas version is a 4.0.0 release candidate (repo head is already rc8).
found_via: GitHub: README Benchmarks section of samizdatco/skia-canvas, followed to samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks results/darwin-arm64/2026-10-01/index.md (raw.githubusercontent.com), while checking JavaScript canvas libraries for the any-language pass

name: @napi-rs/canvas
language: Rust (Skia binding for Node.js via Node-API)
baseline: node-canvas (the npm 'canvas' package v3.2.3, which renders with Cairo)
workload: Same samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks Node.js canvas scripts as skia-canvas (Path2D drawing, Bezier curves, dense line chart, SVG to PNG, scale/rotate images, gradients, text, PDF to PNG, get/put ImageData, cold start), measured against the Cairo-based canvas package.
claimed_speedup: Relative to canvas (Cairo) = 1.0x, @napi-rs/canvas v1.0.10: Path2D 99 ms vs 133 ms = 1.3x; Bezier curves 181 ms vs 418 ms = 2.3x; dense line chart 79 ms vs 135 ms = 1.7x; SVG to PNG 1.4x; scale/rotate images 193 ms vs 819 ms = 4.2x; gradients 25 ms vs 57 ms = 2.3x; text 19 ms vs 24 ms = 1.2x; PDF to PNG 1.1x; get/put ImageData 283 ms vs 272 ms (no gain, 1.0x); cold start 71 ms vs 108 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Node 24.6.0; prebuilt npm packages @napi-rs/canvas v1.0.10 and canvas v3.2.3; native build flags not stated on the results page
hardware: MacBook Air 13-inch (M3, 2024, Mac15,12): Apple M3 2.4 GHz 8 cores, 24 GiB RAM, macOS 15.7.5
tradeoffs: Node.js native addon with zero system dependencies (prebuilt Skia); implements the browser Canvas API plus Path2D/PathKit boolean ops, Lottie via Skottie, AVIF/WebP encoding; no multi-threaded async path like skia-canvas; SVG/PDF export converts to bitmap in the benchmark.
caveats: The table above was run by the author of a competing library (skia-canvas), so it is not first-party for this project, but it is a single run on one laptop. The project's own README also reports 'Draw a House and export to PNG' at 68 ops/s versus node-canvas 60 ops/s and 'Draw Gradient and export to PNG' at 66 versus 56 ops/s on an Apple M3 Max (about 1.13x and 1.18x, derived from page data); the README labels its own row '@napi-rs/skia', an older package name. Speedup mainly reflects Skia versus Cairo, and several rows are near parity (get/put ImageData 1.0x, PDF to PNG 1.1x, text 1.2x). Tier A is generous: prebuilt npm binaries, so compiler and flags are not stated.
found_via: GitHub: README Performance section of Brooooooklyn/canvas, cross-checked against the samizdatco/canvas-benchmarks results page (raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: ImageSharp.Drawing
baseline: Skia via SkiaSharp (BenchmarkDotNet Baseline=true), and System.Drawing (GDI+)
workload: FillParis benchmark: render a 1096x1060 Paris street-map SVG (code comment says 30k paths; release post says 50K fill paths) fill-only with per-path transforms and opacity, using BenchmarkDotNet across SkiaSharp, System.Drawing, ImageSharp.Drawing CPU, CPU retained scene, WebGPU and WebGPU retained scene. The repo also has a FillTiger benchmark.
claimed_speedup: ImageSharp.Drawing 3.1.0 release post (as reported in search-result text): SkiaSharp 103.4 ms, System.Drawing 147.3 ms, ImageSharp.Drawing CPU 43.0 ms, CPU retained scene 11.9 ms, WebGPU 20.0 ms, WebGPU retained scene 5.6 ms. Ratios versus SkiaSharp (derived from page data): CPU 2.4x, CPU retained 8.7x, WebGPU 5.2x, WebGPU retained 18.5x. 3.0.0 post on .NET 8: SkiaSharp 103.165 ms versus CPU 48.544 ms (about 2.1x), retained CPU 17.879 ms (5.8x), WebGPU retained 5.476 ms (about 19x).
compiler_and_flags: .NET 10 (3.1.0 post) and .NET 8 (3.0.0 post) with BenchmarkDotNet; Release flags not seen; benchmark source is tests/ImageSharp.Drawing.Benchmarks/Drawing/FillParis.cs in the repo
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, Windows 11 (3.1.0 post); 3.0.0 post says Windows x64 with .NET 8, CPU model not seen
license: Six Labors Split License 1.0 (not an SPDX id): Apache-2.0 for open-source use, transitive dependency use, for-profit under 1M USD annual revenue and non-profits; paid Six Labors Commercial License otherwise
tradeoffs: .NET only; pure managed CPU rasterizer plus an optional WebGPU backend; retained-scene mode needs the scene to be recorded up front; licence is not OSI-approved for larger commercial users.
caveats: Snippet only: sixlabors.com is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so the numbers come from WebSearch result text of the 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 release posts and were not opened as pages; two snippets agree and the 3.0.0 ratios reproduce from the listed times. The benchmark source (FillParis.cs, SkiaSharp is Baseline=true) was opened on GitHub and compares SkiaSharp, System.Drawing and ImageSharp, but the numbers are not in the repo. The posts are from the vendor that sells the library, so first-party; the path-count wording differs between the code comment (30k) and the post (50K). The SkiaSharp baseline is Skia's CPU raster path reached through a managed wrapper.
found_via: WebSearch: 'SixLabors ImageSharp.Drawing rasterizer performance benchmark vs SkiaSharp vs System.Drawing polygon fill' and 'ImageSharp.Drawing FillParis benchmark'; repo, tests folder and FillParis.cs opened on github.com

name: Marlin renderer (Java 2D)
baseline: OpenJDK 8 Pisces and Oracle JDK 8 Ductus (the Java 2D antialiasing rasterizers)
workload: MapBench 0.4 (Java 2D vector map rendering) at 1, 2 and 4 threads on JDK 8, default profile (one image per iteration) and shared profile (one image per test, 10 s per test).
claimed_speedup: Wiki Benchmarks page: Marlin 0.3 versus OpenJDK 8 Pisces 'score small' Tavg 163.28% (1 thread), 162.93% (2), 164.92% (4); 'score big' 327.59%, 372.77%, 391.64%. Marlin 0.3 versus JDK 8 Ductus 'score small' 96.28% (1 thread), 134.03% (2), 186.95% (4); 'score big' 128.67%, 164.76%, 386.80%. Headline: 'Marlin 0.5.4 is 17% to 25% faster than marlin 0.3 and is as fast as Oracle ductus !'
compiler_and_flags: JDK 8 (Ductus), OpenJDK 8 (Pisces, Marlin); MapBench 0.4; JVM flags not stated on the page
stars_or_usage: 197 stars; default Java 2D antialiasing renderer in OpenJDK 9+ (JEP 265) and in OpenJFX as Marlin-FX
tradeoffs: Java only; no GC pressure thanks to pooled array caches; scales near-linearly across threads where Ductus had synchronised singleton native structures; derived from OpenJDK 8 Pisces source and licensed GPLv2 with Classpath Exception.
caveats: Baselines are Java 2D rasterizers (Pisces, Ductus), not Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, so baseline_in_list is false. The wiki page does not state the CPU model. Percent tables are scores relative to the baseline; reading them as Marlin throughput relative to Pisces/Ductus is my inference (consistent with the headline: roughly parity with Ductus single-threaded, 1.9x at 4 threads, and 1.6x-3.9x over Pisces). Numbers are from the JDK 8 era (2015-2017) and Marlin is now the default renderer, so the Pisces/Ductus incumbents are historical or closed-source. The linked full MapBench result pages are on bourgesl.github.io, which is blocked here, so only the wiki text tables were read. JEP 265 (openjdk.org) is blocked too.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Marlin renderer Java 2D rasterizer faster than Pisces Ductus benchmark github bourgesl'; wiki Benchmarks page read through raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki and github.com

name: tdewolff/canvas
baseline: Cairo and Inkscape (README says 'existing solutions' and names Inkscape and Cairo)
workload: An extreme-case SVG-to-raster conversion described in canvas issue #280 (a very large, complex SVG); the comparison comment itself could not be read.
claimed_speedup: README: 'the rasterizer is highly optimized with ASM' and, for an extreme case, the library is 'at least twice as fast as existing solutions, and can handle bigger images than the likes of Inkscape and Cairo'.
tradeoffs: Pure Go vector graphics with raster, SVG, PDF, EPS, HTML Canvas and Gio outputs; assembly-optimised rasterizer is architecture specific; Fribidi and HarfBuzz can be CGO or native Go.
caveats: Only a README sentence points to issue #280 comment 1995990038, and that comment did not render in WebFetch (only the issue opening text and a 'JSVG takes a second or two' remark were visible), so numbers, hardware and the exact workload are unverified. The separate tdewolff/canvas_benchmarks repo compares polygon boolean operations (Clipper, Clipper2, iOverlay), not rasterization. First-party, no stated methodology, one extreme case.
found_via: GitHub: README of tdewolff/canvas (raw.githubusercontent.com), opened issue #280 and canvas_benchmarks README

name: resvg-js
language: Rust (Node.js and WebAssembly binding of resvg)
baseline: svg2img (canvg plus node-canvas, which is Cairo-based) and sharp (libvips with librsvg)
workload: README 'Sample Benchmark', the 'resize width' suite run with benny: render an SVG to PNG at a different width.
claimed_speedup: resvg-js (Rust) 12 ops/s; sharp 9 ops/s; skr-canvas (Rust) 7 ops/s; svg2img (canvg and node-canvas) 6 ops/s. About 2x svg2img and 1.3x sharp (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: npm i benny@3.x sharp@0.x svg2img@0.x then npm run bench; Node version and build flags not stated
tradeoffs: SVG renderer (resvg on tiny-skia) rather than a general 2D drawing API; Node-API addon plus pure WASM backend that is slower; MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft.
caveats: Weak evidence: README gives integer ops/s for a single SVG and resize with no hardware, Node version or SVG named. The baselines are wrapped Cairo (via node-canvas) and librsvg (via sharp), not Cairo called directly, so baseline_in_list is false. It is an SVG-to-PNG pipeline benchmark, not a pure rasterizer test, and it is a Node binding of the resvg crate (the underlying tiny-skia is already catalogued), so it may fold into a duplicate decision.
found_via: GitHub: README Sample Benchmark section of resvg-js (raw.githubusercontent.com), found while checking resvg descendants for the any-language pass

name: stilus
baseline: golang.org/x/image/vector (the Go project's rasterizer) and gogpu/gg v0.52.5 CPU rasterizer
workload: Synthetic print-style scenes on an A3 landscape page at 150 dpi (2481x1754 px): 2,000 hatch lines and 20,000 short strokes. stilus strokes and fills directly; the x/image/vector run fills the outlines produced by stilus's own stroker, with one vector.Rasterizer sized to each outline's bounding box; gg runs with no clip.
claimed_speedup: README comparison table: 2 000 hatch lines: stilus 70 ms, x/image/vector 33 400 ms, gogpu/gg 14 800 ms; 20 000 short strokes: stilus 55 ms, x/image/vector 111 ms, gogpu/gg 2 090 ms. About 477x and 2.0x versus x/image/vector (derived from page data). Separate 'Numbers' table: stilus 1 core 67 ms (2 000 hatch lines at 0.35 mm) and 41 ms (20 000 short strokes), 4 cores 19 ms and 12 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Go (go.mod says go 1.24; toolchain version for the table not stated); `cd bench && go test -bench .`, comparison source is bench/compare_test.go (separate module)
hardware: 'Same machine' as the Numbers table: cloud Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (exact model not stated), minimum of 15 runs; some speed levers were measured on a Ryzen 7 5800H
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no cgo, no dependencies, builds for all GOOS/GOARCH including js/wasm; zero allocations after warm-up; sparse cost model (edge length plus covered spans); exact-area coverage like FreeType/AGG; optional AVX2/AVX-512 compositing under GOEXPERIMENT=simd; it is only the rasterizer core of a planned PDF renderer (no fonts, colour spaces or display lists).
caveats: The baseline is used in a way that favours stilus: x/image/vector's cost is proportional to the bounding-box area, so long diagonal hatch lines cost it a full box each, which explains the 477x ratio (above 50x, so capped at tier C). It is not compared against Skia, Cairo or Blend2D, so baseline_in_list is false; the README only checks quality against PDFium (mean deviation 0.3-1.5/255, SSIM at least 0.998). First-party, one author, synthetic scenes, CPU model not named exactly, Go toolchain version not stated for the comparison table; benchmark source was skimmed, not run.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/rasterizer?l=go and vector-graphics?l=go, then README Numbers and comparison tables of timzifer/stilus and bench/compare_test.go via raw.githubusercontent.com
